prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My first week in Cambridge a car full of white boys tried to run me off the road, and spit through the window, open to ask directions. I was always asking directions and always driving: to an Armenian market in Watertown to buy figs and string cheese, apricots, dark spices and olives from barrels, tubes of paste with unreadable Arabic labels. I ate stuffed grape leaves and watched my lips swell in the mirror. The floors of my apartment would never come clean. Whenever I saw other colored people in bookshops, or museums, or cafeterias, I’d gasp, smile shyly, but they’d disappear before I spoke. What would I have said to them? Come with me? Take me home? Are you my mother? No. I sat alone in countless Chinese restaurants eating almond cookies, sipping tea with spoons and spoons of sugar. Popcorn and coffee was dinner. When I fainted from migraine in the grocery store, a Portuguese man above me mouthed: “No breakfast.” He gave me orange juice and chocolate bars. The color red sprang into relief singing Wagner’s Walküre. Entire tribes gyrated and drummed in my head. I learned the samba from a Brazilian man so tiny, so festooned with glitter I was certain that he slept inside a filigreed, Fabergé egg. No one at the door: no salesmen, Mormons, meter readers, exterminators, no Harriet Tubman, no one. Red notes sounding in a grey trolley town.

**Polished Version:**

During my first week in Cambridge, a car carrying a group of young white men attempted to force me off the road, spitting through my open window as I leaned out to ask for directions. I was perpetually behind the wheel and perpetually lost, driving to an Armenian market in Watertown to acquire figs, string cheese, apricots, dark spices, olives from wooden barrels, and tubes of paste bearing unreadable Arabic script. I dined on stuffed grape leaves and watched my lips swell in the reflection of the mirror. 

The floors of my apartment refused to ever come clean. Whenever I caught sight of other people of color in bookstores, museums, or cafeterias, I would gasp and offer a hesitant smile, yet they always vanished before I could speak. What could I have possibly said to them? *Come with me? Take me home? Are you my mother?* No. 

Instead, I sat alone in countless Chinese restaurants, eating almond cookies and sipping tea sweetened with spoonfuls upon spoonfuls of sugar. Popcorn and coffee constituted dinner. When a migraine caused me to collapse in the grocery store, a Portuguese man hovered above me, softly mouthing, “No breakfast.” He sustained me with orange juice and chocolate bars. A vivid shade of red sprang into relief, resounding like Wagner’s *Walküre*, while entire tribes seemed to gyrate and drum inside my head. 

Later, I learned the samba from a Brazilian man—a figure so diminutive and so thoroughly festooned with glitter that I felt certain he slept inside a filigreed Fabergé egg. Yet no one ever knocked on my door: no salesmen, no Mormons, no meter readers, no exterminators, no Harriet Tubman—no one at all. Just vibrant red notes echoing through a muted, gray trolley town.

Here is a complete rewrite of the text, preserving all original facts while using entirely different sentence structures and vocabulary:

Shortly after arriving in Cambridge, I was targeted by a carload of young white men who tried to push my vehicle off the street; as I rolled down my window to ask for directions, they spat inside. Navigating was a constant struggle, and I spent hours behind the wheel, frequently lost, driving to an Armenian shop in Watertown. There, I stocked up on dried figs, braided cheese, apricots, deep-colored spices, olives scooped from wooden tubs, and squeeze tubes filled with paste labeled in Arabic script I couldn't read. After consuming rice-stuffed vine leaves, I stood in front of a mirror and watched my lips puff up from an allergic reaction. 

In my flat, the floors stayed perpetually dirty regardless of my efforts. On the rare occasions I spotted other non-white individuals in art galleries, bookshops, or lunchrooms, I would catch my breath and offer a timid grin, but they always vanished before I could initiate a conversation. I questioned what I would have even uttered to them—would I have begged them to leave with me, asked to be taken home, or inquired if they were my mother? Obviously not. Instead, I dined by myself at innumerable Chinese eateries, snacking on almond biscuits and washing them down with hot tea heavily laden with sugar. On many nights, my evening meal was nothing more than coffee paired with popped corn. 

When a blinding headache caused me to pass out in a supermarket aisle, a Portuguese bystander hovered over me, silently shaping the phrase "No breakfast" with his lips. He brought me back to my senses with citrus juice and candy bars. Vivid crimson hues suddenly flared in my mind to the dramatic operatic strains of Wagner's *Walküre*, accompanied by inner visions of dancing, drumming tribes. Later, I took samba lessons from a diminutive gentleman from Brazil; he was so tiny and adorned with so much shimmer that I imagined him resting at night within a jewel-encrusted, ornate egg. 

Through it all, no visitors ever knocked at my entrance—no door-to-door vendors, religious recruiters, utility inspectors, pest technicians, or iconic saviors. Passionate, vibrant sounds reverberated through a drab, transit-dominated city.
outputs.L3:
My arrival in Cambridge was marked not by the quiet grandeur of its ancient architecture, but by a sudden, jarring act of malice. During my very first week, the latent tension of the city exploded into explicit racial hostility when a group of white boys deliberately tried to run me off the road, capping their violent harassment by spitting at me. The incident left me shaken to my core, exposing an underlying toxicity in a place I had hoped might be a refuge.

In the wake of this cruelty, a profound sense of isolation settled over me. I moved through the city like a ghost, desperately seeking a sense of belonging or a shared glance of understanding. I found myself searching the crowds for other people of color, aching to bridge the gulf of my loneliness. Yet, they always seemed like mirages—disappearing down narrow alleys or boarding passing buses just before I could reach out or speak to them. 

This deep social exile soon began to erode my physical well-being. Living in total solitude, I lost the motivation to care for myself, frequently skipping meals and neglecting basic nutrition. My body eventually buckled under the weight of this neglect. The exhaustion culminating in a blinding, agonizing migraine that caused me to faint onto the cold floor of my room, alone in the dark.

Yet, amidst the overwhelming darkness of this period, brief flashes of warmth and color occasionally pierced the gloom. I experienced unexpected moments of genuine human connection with other outsiders who crossed my path. There was the quiet kindness of a Portuguese man who stepped in to help me when I was at my lowest, and the irrepressible joy of a Brazilian man who, for a few fleeting hours, filled my quiet world with music and taught me the rhythmic steps of the samba. In these rare interactions, the world briefly felt vibrant, compassionate, and alive.

Ultimately, however, these moments were merely brief pauses in an overarching narrative of solitude. As soon as those fleeting companions departed, the vibrant colors washed away, leaving me once again trapped in a persistent state of deep alienation—an outsider adrift in a cold, grey, and relentlessly unwelcoming city.
outputs.L4:
Cambridge presented itself in shades of wet slate and institutional grey. The historic city, famed for its towering spires and quiet intellect, felt to me like a fortress built entirely of cold stone and closed doors. In my first few months, the isolation was not merely physical; it was heavy, ambient, and sharp. 

Racial hostility in Cambridge rarely roared; instead, it murmured in quiet, biting microaggressions. It was in the sudden, defensive clutching of a handbag when I stepped into an elevator, the frost in a shopkeeper’s voice that thawed only when a white customer stepped up behind me, and the lingering, questioning stares on the narrow pavements that silently asked what right I had to occupy space here. The city was a masterclass in polite exclusion, leaving me feeling stripped of my identity, invisible yet uncomfortably scrutinized.

To survive the suffocating monochrome of my routine, I began to hunt for color. 

My search drew me away from the manicured lawns of the university centers toward the cramped, bustling fringes of the town. I sought out the small, independent ethnic grocery stores hidden in side streets—tiny sanctuaries of survival tucked into the city’s cracks. Stepping across the threshold of a small international market was like breaking through ice into warm water. 

Here, the air was dense with the smell of home: the sharp, earthy bite of raw ginger, the sweet hum of frying plantains, the dusty warmth of ground cumin and cardamom, and the rich, oily scent of roasted coffee beans. Shelves were stacked high with sacks of jasmine rice, tins of coconut milk, and glass jars of dark, fiery chili pastes. 

In these spaces, I did not just look for food; I looked for people. I looked for the familiar rich browns and warm bronzes of skin that matched my own. We were a quiet, informal diaspora, scattered across a city that refused to see us. In the aisles of these markets, our eyes would meet over crates of bitter melon or fresh guavas. We rarely spoke at length, but there was a silent, profound geography in those glances—an unspoken acknowledgement that said: *I know the chill you just came in from. I feel it, too.*

One rainy Tuesday, when the weight of the city felt particularly unbearable, I spent an hour in a tiny, overcrowded Afro-Caribbean corner shop, simply inhaling the warmth. I picked up a small bag of dried hibiscus flowers, desperate to brew something that tasted like sunlight. 

When I brought it to the counter, the middle-aged woman behind the register looked at my soaked coat and the tired shadow beneath my eyes. She scanned the bag, then reached beneath the counter and pulled out a small, warm pastry wrapped in wax paper. She slid it into my bag alongside the hibiscus.

"You look like you're carrying the whole sky on your shoulders today, sweetheart," she said softly, her voice rich with a deep, melodic accent that felt like a thick wool blanket. "Eat this while it’s hot."

I didn't know her name, and she didn't know mine. I walked back out into the rain, sitting on a wooden bench beneath the dripping canopy of an ancient oak tree, eating the warm, spiced pastry. Tears pricked my eyes, hot against the cold air.

That small act of unexpected tenderness did not magically transform Cambridge. The city remained largely unwelcoming, and my apartment stayed quiet and empty. I was still profoundly lonely, suspended between a life I had left behind and a place that refused to make room for me. I had not yet found a community, nor a true sense of home.

Yet, as I finished the pastry and wiped the rainwater from my face, something inside me settled. Those brief, vibrant encounters—the burst of saffron yellow on a market shelf, the nod of recognition from a stranger on a bus, the unprompted warmth of a shopkeeper—were small, fierce coals. They were enough to keep a fire burning inside me, proving that even in the coldest city, vitality and grace could still be found, one small spark at a time.
outputs.L5:
Along the winding banks of the Charles River, just west of Boston, lies a vibrant corridor where deep history and rich culture intertw. As you travel down Mount Auburn Street, moving seamlessly from the bustling academic avenues of **Cambridge** into the welcoming neighborhoods of **Watertown**, you are stepping into one of the most significant hubs of the **Armenian** diaspora in the Western world.

For over a century, Watertown has served as a cultural sanctuary and heartland for Armenian-Americans. Following the tragic events of the Armenian Genocide in the early 20th century, thousands of survivors found a new beginning in this Massachusetts town, drawn by industrial jobs and the promise of safety. Over the decades, they transformed Watertown into a flourishing community. Today, a stroll down its streets offers an immersive sensory experience: the rich aroma of freshly baked lavash and lamajoun drifts from local staples like Massis Bakery and Sevan Bakery, while the Armenian Museum of America stands as a proud guardian of the nation’s ancient art, textiles, and history.

Yet, this Armenian heritage is not contained within Watertown's borders alone; it shares a symbiotic relationship with neighboring Cambridge. The intellectual and academic spirit of Cambridge has long amplified Armenian culture and scholarship. Harvard University, located in the heart of Cambridge, established the Mashtots Chair in Armenian Studies in 1955, making it a world-renowned center for research into Armenian language, history, and literature. Scholars, artists, and students frequently move between the quiet, book-lined archives of Cambridge and the lively, community-centered streets of Watertown.

Even the geography reflects this deep connection. Mount Auburn Cemetery, a historic landmark straddling the border of both cities, serves as the final resting place for prominent Armenian intellectuals, artists, and community leaders who shaped the diaspora's identity. 

Together, Cambridge and Watertown represent a unique dual legacy for the Armenian-American experience. While Watertown provides the soul, traditional flavors, and close-knit community ties, Cambridge offers the scholarly platform that ensures Armenian history and contemporary thought are shared with the world. Bound by proximity and a shared history, these two cities continue to honor a resilient culture that thrives at the intersection of memory and modernity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of creative nonfiction about feeling isolated as a person of color in a new city, using vivid sensory details, food, and surreal imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
The city was drawn in HB pencil: graphite skies, damp pavement, and towers of brushed zinc that absorbed the daylight without returning a single spark. In this new northern grid, I moved like an ink spill on a freshly laundered sheet—hyper-visible, yet completely unread.

On the streetcar, the commuters glided past me like paper cutouts. Their hair was the color of oat milk; their linen coats bled into the fog. When they looked at me, their eyes didn't rest; they slid over my brown skin as if it were oiled glass, searching for a familiar geometry and finding none. I felt my own borders softening, as if the cold damp was slowly leaching the pigment from my knuckles, turning my marrow into gray chalk.

By November, the isolation had a physical weight, cold and flat like a copper coin pressed beneath my tongue. 

I retreated to my kitchen, a white porcelain box that smelled of industrial bleach and wet wool. I needed to anchor myself before the city washed me out entirely. I pulled out the iron pot—the only object in my apartment that carried weight—and set it on the flame. 

I began the ritual of reclamation. I cracked open dried guajillo chiles, their skins rustling like dead autumn leaves, releasing a sharp, dusty sweetness that cut through the room’s sterile air. I dropped them into hot water, watching them swell back into leathery life, turning the liquid into a dark, translucent garnet. In the blender, they whirred with charred tomatoes, garlic cloves that burst under the flat of my knife like small white teeth, a stick of cinnamon, and a square of unsweetened Mexican chocolate, dark as obsidian.

When the purée hit the hot lard in the pot, the kitchen erupted. 

The sound was a throat clearing, a loud, spitting refusal to be quiet. A cloud of bloom rose—chile, clove, cumin, and rich cocoa—so thick I could taste it on the back of my teeth before I even dipped a spoon. It wasn't just steam; it was an atmosphere. For a moment, the white walls dissolved. The ceiling stretched upward into a indigo night, and the linoleum floor gave way to red dirt warm enough to bake bread.

I simmered the mole until it thickened into molten earth, slick with red oil that pooled on the surface like miniature, glowing suns. 

Sitting alone at the small laminate table, I dipped a folded tortilla into the dark sauce. The first bite was an execution of the grayness outside. Heat bloomed behind my eyes—not just the bite of capsaicin, but the deep, layered warmth of a hundred summers I hadn't spent here. The sweet bitterness of the cacao coated my palate, heavy and ancient. 

Outside my window, the city pressed its pale, wet face against the glass, trying to look in. But the glass had fogged over with spice and moisture. My skin, flushed hot and copper from the heat of the chiles, glowed in the dim kitchen. I swallowed, feeling the dark thread of the sauce trace its way down my chest, lighting a small, stubborn fire in the middle of all that ice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a passage in the style of a literary memoir detailing a narrator's lonely first week living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, blending experiences of alienation with rich sensory descriptions of food and music.
counterfactuals.output:
The silence of my third-floor walk-up on Linnaean Street had a physical weight, thick as the dust settling on the unpainted floorboards. It was my fifth day in Cambridge, a city that seemed to have been constructed entirely out of red brick, damp ivy, and a cold, polite indifference. I knew no one. My apartment contained only a rolled-out futon, a stack of thrift-store paperbacks, and a yellowing refrigerator that hummed a single, sharp B-flat across the empty rooms.

To escape the room’s asphyxiating quiet, I learned to eat as a form of displacement. Food became my only tether to the tactile world. On Tuesday night, driven out by the encroaching twilight, I wandered down to a basement noodle shop near Harvard Square. The air inside was dense with the clouds of boiling starch and roasted pork fat. I sat at a narrow laminate counter, shoulder-to-shoulder with strangers who stared resolutely into their phones, and ordered a bowl of shoyu ramen. 

When it arrived, the broth was an opaque, amber mirror, gleaming with tiny beads of sesame oil. I drank it fast, desperate for the heat. The flavor was deep, soy-heavy and rich with bone marrow, leaving a slick, savory film on my lips that felt almost like a comfort, a temporary shield against the October chill waiting for me outside. I chewed the thick, springy noodles in rhythm with the kitchen’s clatter, anchoring myself in the sharp, clean sting of pickled bamboo shoots and the velvety, unctuous give of a soft-boiled egg. It was a purely solitary communion—eating to fill an emptiness that had very little to do with hunger.

Leaving the warmth of the shop, I descended into the subterranean cavern of the Harvard T station, where the alienation of the city always seemed most acute. But that evening, the echo of the turnstiles was swallowed by music. 

A street musician—an elderly man in a frayed tweed coat—was playing a cello in the tiled concourse. He was playing Bach’s Cello Suite No. 1 in G Major, the notes rising and tumbling against the curved, salt-glazed walls. The sound was low, woody, and intensely resonant, vibrating directly through the soles of my boots. I stopped by a tiled pillar, watching the commuters stream past him, a river of dark wool coats and leather satchels, nobody stopping, nobody looking. 

The music was exquisite, yet it made my loneliness feel vast and architectural. The prelude’s arpeggios rolled out like a tide, gorgeous and utterly indifferent to whether anyone was listening. I stood there for twenty minutes, my back pressed against the cold tiles, listening to the cello mourn and celebrate in the same breath. It echoed the double edge of my new life: the intoxicating freedom of being completely unknown, paired with the terrifying realization that if I were to disappear into the Charles River that night, the city would go on humming in B-flat without missing a beat.

Later, walking back under the arches of the oak trees along Mass Ave, the music seemed to linger in the damp air, blending with the smell of woodsmoke and decaying leaves. I bought a single Macoun apple from a late-night corner market—crisp, tart, and smelling of autumn orchards—and ate it on the dark walk home. Each bite snapped sharply in the quiet street, a small, vibrant sound of survival in a city that had not yet learned my name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a vignette about an outsider moving to a grey northeastern town who experiences racial hostility, severe loneliness, and strange, fleeting encounters with strangers.
counterfactuals.output:
In Oakhaven, grey was not a color; it was a texture. It clung to the salt-bitten clapboard houses, settled in the slush that clogged the gutters, and hung over the Atlantic like a damp, wool blanket that never quite dried. 

Amara had been here three weeks, long enough for her skin to feel perpetually chilled, long enough to realize she was the only Black woman within thirty miles. 

Her isolation was a physical weight. It lived in her tiny, rented apartment above a closed-down bait shop, where the radiator clanked uselessly against the coastal draft. But the cold inside was nothing compared to the cold outside.

When she walked down Main Street, the town shrank back. It wasn't always loud, though yesterday a rusted pickup truck had slowed to a crawl beside her, its engine gunning, the driver—a man with a face like cured leather—spitting out the window before yelling, "Lost your way, girl?" The word *girl* had echoed off the wet brick buildings, heavy with a sharp, ancient malice. 

More often, the hostility was quiet. It was the way the cashier at the greasy-spoon diner would suddenly forget how to speak when Amara approached, setting her coffee down with enough force to spill it, refusing to touch her hand when handing back change. The coins were always dropped onto the Formica counter, sliding into puddle of melted salt. It was the stares from porch windows, curtains snapping shut the moment she looked up. They watched her as if she were a inkblot on a clean white page, a smudge that needed scraping off.

By her fourth week, silence became her primary language. She spoke only to order groceries or pay for gas. Her voice began to feel small and papery in her throat.

Then came the strange ones.

The town seemed to generate ghosts that hadn't quite finished dying. One dusk, while walking along the rocky spit of land that jutted into the dark water, Amara met an old woman. She wore a heavy moth-eaten coat and sat on a overturned lobster crate, staring into the fog. 

As Amara passed, the woman reached out, her gnarled fingers catching the hem of Amara’s jacket. Amara froze, her pulse leaping into her ears.

"You’re too bright," the woman rasped. Her eyes were milky with cataracts, but she stared directly into Amara’s face. "The fog doesn't like things it can't bleach. It’ll come for your eyes first."

Amara pulled away, her heart hammering against her ribs. When she turned back ten paces later, the mist had swallowed the crate, the woman, and the shore entirely.

Two nights later, under the flickering fluorescent light of the town's only 24-hour laundromat, a boy no older than ten appeared. He was soaked to the bone, his clothes clinging to his thin frame, though it wasn't raining. He didn't have any laundry. He simply sat on top of a whirring dryer, swinging his legs, watching the clothes tumble in circles.

Amara kept her distance, folding her clothes with agonizing care. 

"My uncle says you came from the sun," the boy said suddenly. His voice was flat, uninflected. 

Amara looked up, holding a folded sweater like a shield. "I came from Atlanta."

The boy tilted his head, his dark eyes wide and unblinking. "He says if we keep you here long enough, the winter will drink you up until you look like the rest of us. Chalk." He smiled, but his lips were blue. Before she could answer, he slid off the dryer, walked out into the freezing night, and was gone into the darkness before the automatic doors had even hissed shut.

That night, Amara lay in bed, listening to the ocean drag the gravel back and forth along the shore. The room smelled of wet wool, salt, and her own profound, suffocating solitude. She looked at her hands in the dark, pressing her thumbs against her knuckles, checking to see if she was still solid, still warm, still real in a place that wanted so desperately to wash her away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a excerpt for a story that captures the disorienting feeling of moving somewhere new alone. Include specific local details like driving to an Armenian market in Watertown, eating in empty Chinese restaurants, and having a migraine in a grocery store.
counterfactuals.output:
In the first three weeks, my world shrunk to the radius of my headlights and the blue dot pulsing uncertainty on my phone’s map. Boston was a maze of aggressive rotaries and street names that changed every three blocks without warning, and I was a ghost drifting through it, completely tethered to nothing.

Time moved in weird, elastic fits. On a rainy Tuesday, desperate for a reason to leave an apartment that still smelled like the previous tenant’s radiator dust, I drove out to Watertown. I was looking for a specific kind of bread I’d read about online, but mostly I just wanted to be somewhere that required focus. The rain smeared the brake lights ahead into long, ruby streaks on the asphalt. Inside the Armenian market off Mount Auburn Street, the air was dense and warm, thick with the intoxicating, dry-spiced smell of roasted nuts, sumac, and fresh za’atar. Old men chatted over crates of pomegranates in a language that felt like a thick velvet curtain drawn between them and me. I hovered in the narrow aisles, my fingers tracing the cold plastic wrapped around braided string cheese and tins of grape leaves, feeling terrifyingly invisible. I bought a bag of dried apricots I didn't want, just to prove to the cashier that I existed.

Hunger was the only thing that kept time. But eating felt shameful when there was no one across the table to split the silence with. I found refuge in the quiet, cavernous Chinese restaurants tucked into strip malls along the edges of the city—places with faded gold dragon wallpaper and sticky vinyl booths. I’d go at four in the afternoon, during the dead hour between lunch and dinner. The only sound would be the hum of the ice machine, the soft clatter of a porcelain spoon against a bowl of hot and sour soup, and the dull thud of my own heart. The waiters left me alone, dropping off tea in small, handleless cups that burned my fingers, letting me sit until the streetlights flickered on outside.

The peak of the dislocation came on a Thursday night inside a suburban Stop & Shop. 

It started behind my left eye—a tiny, jagged worm of silver light that fluttered across my vision while I was staring at a wall of salad dressings. I tried to blink it away, but the aura expanded, turning the edges of the world into a shimmering, fractured stained-glass window. A migraine. 

Within minutes, the grocery store became a chamber of horror. The endless rows of overhead fluorescent lights didn't just illuminate the aisles; they screamed. They buzzed with a low, electrical violence that vibrated straight into my jawline. I stood paralyzed in the pain-reliever aisle, the air smelling intensely of cold floor wax and bleach. My depth perception evaporated. The yellow boxes of Nurofen looked miles away, then violently close. 

I couldn't remember how to read the labels. The words turned into alien glyphs. Panic, cold and greasy, pooled in my throat. I had no one to call. No partner waiting at home, no friend to drive fifteen minutes to come fetch me, no mother down the street. If I passed out here, on the polished linoleum next to the band-aids, I would just be an inconvenience for an eighteen-year-old clerk stocking shelves.

I clutched the shelf, pressed my palm hard against my throbbing temple, and forced my eyes down to the icy tile floor. I took one agonizingly slow step toward the register, praying my legs would remember how to walk in a city that didn't know my name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a poetic prose fragment exploring themes of displacement and identity that includes the following motifs: buying figs and olives, fainting, Wagner's Walküre, a flamboyant Brazilian man, and the color red.
counterfactuals.output:
I am translating myself again, syllable by heavy syllable, under a sky the color of bruised tin. At the damp street market, my fingers trace the wrinkled, briny skins of black olives and the swollen, dark flesh of early figs. I trade foreign coins for these small, edible memories, trying to anchor a name that no longer sounds like mine in a city that refuses to learn it. 

Beside me stands Marcelo, a glorious, uncontainable storm of a man from Salvador da Bahia. Draped in a trailing scarf of violent, unapologetic red that bleeds through the northern mist, he moves like a burst of impossible summer. He laughs, a rich, brassy sound like scarlet birds taking flight, and presses a fig to his lips. "Back home, *meu amor*," he purrs, his identity an open, dancing flame while mine is a wet box of matches, "we do not buy the sun in paper bags; we let it ruin us."

Suddenly, from the open doorway of a secondhand vinyl shop across the cobblestones, the tempest erupts. The frantic, riding brass of Wagner’s *Die Walküre* pours into the narrow street—a thunderous, storm-swept Valhalla crashing against the smell of brine and crushed fruit. The brass horns swell, heroic and terrifying, demanding a homeland I do not possess, summoning tragic deities over the grey market stalls. 

The contrast fractures something fragile behind my ribs. The music rises, the Valkyries gallop through the fog, and Marcelo’s red scarf flashes in my periphery like a soaring flame. The world tilts on its axis; the sticky sweetness in my mouth turns to ash. I am nowhere. I am everyone I have ever left behind. The sky rushes down, choked with brass and crimson, and as my knees buckle, the dark swoops in to swallow the noise, folding me back into the silent, placeless earth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
